correctness.rationale: The nonlinear solution follows from the linear reciprocal equation. The source's scalar finite Carleman section is upper bidiagonal, and backward variation of constants gives the stated binomial formula for every lifted degree and the geometric first-component formula. Its exact remainder gives the finite-horizon iff condition. At \(R=1\), one-variable differentiation gives the unique maximizer \(x_N\) and the \(u_0/(2eN)\) asymptotic. Under the source's rescaling equation, the alternating test vector has Rayleigh quotient \(\frac N2[(c-a)N-(a+c)]\), positive for \(N>(R+3)/(R-1)\). Constant rescaling leaves \(R\) and the decoded truncation invariant.

value.rationale: The anchor explicitly uses finite-horizon numerics beyond \(R=1\) to motivate stronger-nonlinearity fast-forwarding. A sharp boundary example is therefore directly motivated. The accepted theorem shows that a globally stable dissipative scalar flow can still lose Carleman convergence after an explicit time when \(R>1\), identifies the critical \(R=1\) algebraic law, and proves eventual loss of the lifted dissipativity needed by the fast-forwarding solver. This separates finite-horizon beyond-threshold success from a universal long-time extension.
